questions.stem: A scheduled agent job must not run twice concurrently if a previous run is still in progress. Where should that constraint live?

options.text: In the prompt, asking the agent to check whether another instance is running.
In the scheduler or orchestrator — a concurrency limit or lock outside the agent process.
In `CLAUDE.md`.
Nowhere; concurrent runs are harmless.

questions.explanation: Mutual exclusion is an orchestration property. The agent cannot reliably observe or enforce it, and by the time it could, the second run has already started doing work.

distractor_notes.D: Two runs writing the same branch is a real conflict.

analogy.text: It is `concurrencyPolicy: Forbid` on a CronJob. The controller enforces it, not the workload.

questions.stem: An agent opens 40 pull requests a week and reviewers cannot keep up, so PRs are merged with cursory review. What is the correct intervention?

options.text: Hire more reviewers.
Reduce throughput to what review capacity can actually absorb, and raise the bar for what the agent may open a PR about.
Enable auto-merge on agent PRs.
Ask the agent to review its own pull requests.

questions.explanation: Generation capacity that exceeds review capacity does not create value — it creates unreviewed changes with a review-shaped ritual in front of them. Throttle at the source until the human gate is real again.

distractor_notes.A: Sometimes right, rarely available, and it does not address a generator that can outpace any team.
distractor_notes.D: Self-review does not provide the independence the gate exists for.

analogy.text: Arrival rate above service rate means an unbounded queue. You fix it at the arrival side or the queue eats the system.

questions.stem: A CI runner exports 30 environment variables, including production database credentials, and the agent step only needs a GitHub token. What should change?

options.text: Nothing; the agent will ignore variables it does not need.
Scope the step's environment to the single credential it needs, so the others are simply not present in that process.
Add a `CLAUDE.md` rule not to read environment variables.
Rename the variables so they look unimportant.

questions.explanation: Anything in the process environment is reachable by any command the agent runs. Least privilege here is cheap and absolute: inject only the credential the step requires.

distractor_notes.A: Availability is exposure, regardless of intent.
distractor_notes.C: Advisory, and irrelevant to a subprocess that inherits the environment.

analogy.text: It is scoping a task role per task definition instead of attaching one god-role to the whole cluster.

questions.stem: A pipeline needs the agent to return a machine-readable verdict. Which prompt design is most reliable?

options.text: Ask for a summary and parse the prose with a regular expression.
Specify the exact JSON schema, show one example, and instruct that the response contain nothing but that JSON.
Ask it to 'return JSON' with no schema.
Ask for a yes or no and check the first word.

questions.explanation: Reliable structured output comes from stating the schema, demonstrating it, and constraining the response envelope. An unspecified 'return JSON' produces valid JSON with a different shape every time, which is the harder bug to notice.

distractor_notes.D: Loses all reasoning and fails on any hedged answer.

questions.stem: In a standard SDLC, at which point does an agent reviewer deliver the highest value per token spent?

options.text: After deployment, reviewing production incidents.
On the pull request, before human review — the change is small, self-contained, and the cost of a fix is still low.
During quarterly planning.
On the whole repository, nightly, regardless of what changed.

questions.explanation: A PR is the ideal unit of agent review: bounded diff, clear intent, and a moment when fixing something is a comment rather than a rollback. Whole-repository sweeps re-analyse unchanged code every night and mostly rediscover the same findings.

distractor_notes.A: Valuable, but far past the cheapest fix point.

analogy.text: The classic curve: a defect found at review costs a fraction of the same defect found in production. Agents do not change the curve; they let you sample it more often.

questions.stem: Two pipeline stages both need the agent's findings. What is the cleanest hand-off?

options.text: Re-run the agent in the second stage with the same prompt.
Write the structured result to a build artefact in stage one and read it in stage two.
Pass the full transcript as a command-line argument.
Store it in a global environment variable.

questions.explanation: Artefacts are the pipeline's own hand-off mechanism: durable, inspectable, and free of a second inference bill. Re-running costs money and may produce a different answer, which is worse than either outcome alone.

distractor_notes.A: Pays twice for a possibly different result.
distractor_notes.C: Argument length limits and quoting misery.
distractor_notes.D: Environment variables do not reliably cross stage boundaries.

questions.stem: An automation runs two steps: classify 10,000 log lines into known categories, then design a remediation plan for the top failure. What is the sensible model strategy?

options.text: Use the most capable model for both, for consistency.
Use a fast, inexpensive model for the bulk classification and a more capable model for the design step.
Use the cheapest model for both to minimise cost.
Alternate models randomly to average out weaknesses.

questions.explanation: Route by task difficulty. Bulk classification into a known taxonomy is a well-specified, high-volume job; architectural design is exactly where capability pays. Uniform routing overpays on one step or under-delivers on the other.

distractor_notes.A: Pays premium rates for mechanical labelling.
distractor_notes.C: Saves pennies on the step where quality actually matters.

analogy.text: It is instance-type selection. You do not run a batch ETL and a latency-critical API on the same instance family just for tidiness.

questions.stem: An agent step reports success but the change it claims to have made is not in the diff. What should the pipeline have done to catch this?

options.text: Trusted the agent's summary, since it has visibility into its own actions.
Verified the claim independently — assert the diff is non-empty and that the tests covering the change pass — rather than accepting a self-report.
Asked the agent to double-check its own work.
Logged the summary for later reading.

questions.explanation: A claim is not evidence. Pipelines should assert on observable state — the diff, the test result, the artefact — so a confident but incorrect summary cannot pass a gate.

distractor_notes.A: Self-report is the thing under suspicion.
distractor_notes.D: Detection after the fact, not prevention.

analogy.text: It is why CI runs the tests rather than trusting the PR description's claim that they pass.
